title: Write Better Prompts for AI Assistants
subtitle: A 90-minute self-paced course for people who use AI assistants at work

audience.persona: Office professionals new to AI assistants
audience.prior_knowledge: Has used a chat assistant a few times; no technical background
audience.needs: Gets generic or off-target answers and rewrites them by hand

outcomes.text: Write prompts that produce usable answers for everyday work tasks on the first try
Critique prompts written by others against the prompt checklist

objectives.text: Identify the four parts of an effective prompt: task, context, format and examples
Explain how added context and examples change an assistant's answer

assessment.stem: Which part of a prompt tells the assistant how the answer should be laid out?
feedback: The task says what to do, not how to present it.
Context gives background, such as audience and purpose.
Right. Format covers length, structure and style of the answer.
Examples show a sample, but the layout instruction itself is the format.

assessment.stem: Two colleagues ask for 'a summary of this report'. One adds 'for our CFO, who cares about cost'. Why does the second get a more useful answer?
options: Longer prompts always produce better answers
The assistant can choose what to keep based on who will read it
Mentioning a job title switches the assistant into a business mode
The second prompt is more polite
feedback: Length alone doesn't help; relevant detail does.
Right. Knowing the reader and their priority tells the assistant what matters.
There is no special mode; the extra context is what changes the answer.
Politeness has little effect on relevance.

assessment.stem: Showing the assistant one example of the output you want usually makes its answer closer to what you need.
assessment.feedback: Examples are one of the strongest signals of what 'good' looks like.

objectives.text: Rewrite a vague request as a four-part prompt for a real work task
Diagnose why a prompt produced an off-target answer
Judge which of two prompts better fits a task, using the prompt checklist
Design a reusable prompt template for a recurring task in your own job

activities.title: Rewrite three real requests
activities.instructions: Pick three requests you sent to an assistant this month. Rewrite each with task, context, format and examples, run both versions, and note what changed.

activities.title: Prompt clinic
activities.instructions: For each of the three before/after pairs provided, name the missing part that caused the weak answer, then use the checklist to decide which prompt is better and why.

activities.title: Draft your first template
activities.instructions: Take your best rewrite from the first activity and turn the specifics into [placeholders] so you can reuse it next week. Save it where you will find it.

assessment.stem: Your manager asks for a short update on a delayed project. Which prompt applies the four-part method best?
options: Write a project update for my manager that is detailed, comprehensive and covers every single part of the project.
Write a 5-line update for my manager on the 2-week delay, its cause (vendor) and new date, like this: [paste].
You are the world's best writer. Write an amazing, impressive project update that my manager will love.
Write a project update about the delay for my manager. Make it good, clear, professional and not too long.
feedback: 'Detailed and comprehensive' conflicts with a short update and adds no facts.
Right. It has the task, context (reader, delay, cause), format (5 lines) and an example.
Hype words aren't context; the assistant still doesn't know the facts.
Better, but 'good' and 'not too long' leave the length and the facts to guesswork.

assessment.stem: A prompt asked 'Draft an email to the client about the invoice' and the assistant wrote a friendly reminder, but you needed to dispute an overcharge. What is the most likely cause?
options: The assistant ignored the task it was given in the prompt
The prompt was missing context about the situation and goal
The prompt needed a format instruction for the email layout
Assistants can't write emails about money or invoices well
feedback: It did draft the email; it just guessed the purpose.
Right. Without the dispute and the goal, a reminder is the most common guess.
A format instruction would change layout, not the purpose of the email.
Assistants handle emails well when they know the situation.

final_assessment.stem: Choose a task you do every week. Design a reusable prompt template for it, test it twice, and write 3-5 sentences judging how well it worked against the checklist and what you would change.

rubric.excellent: All four parts present; placeholders make it reusable
Two real runs shown, with the outputs
Uses checklist items to justify a specific improvement
